full_judgment:
Leave was granted to examine the question whether the learned Judge of the High Court Division was correct in holding that a subsequent transferee from a person claiming benefit under a document executed by a pardanashin lady as not fastened with burden of proof to show that the lady had independent advice and she properly understood the terms of the deeds before she executed the same. 

 5. To make the disposition by a pardanashin lady a valid one it must be proved that the disposition was substantially understood and it was really the mental set of the person who made it. The rule of law as indicated above is an exception to the general rule the law presumes prima facie in favour of the deeds duly executed, inasmuch as such transactions can be challenged only on the ground of fraud, coercion, undue influence, etc. or on the allegation of bad faith. The rule of section 111 of the Evidence Act, which provides that where there is a question as to the good faith of a transaction between the parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is no the party who is in a position of active confidence. Relationship between the pardanashin woman and the person in fiduciary relationship, who is the done, raises the presumption of influence upon the pardanashin lady and the burden is upon the done to show that the act was spontaneous. 

 6. Once it is shown that the impugned disposition was by a pardanashin woman the burden lies upon the party or parties who set up and rely on the impugn& deed of disposition to show that the deed had been explained to and understood by the party under the disability. Thus, so far as the burden to prove that the pardanashin woman had full knowledge and comprehension about the terms of the disposition, and that it was her mental act, is upon those who want to uphold the disposition. In the cases of Ruhulla V. Hassanlli Begumia, AIR 1928 P.C. 303 this rule was reiterated by Lord Atkin. He observed as follows: 

 7. For the legal position of the question of burden of proof there are innumerable decisions of the superior Courts, out of which  only a few have been cited above. It appears that the consistent view is that the burden of proof rests noon the person who claims benefit under transection entered into with a pardanashin woman to establish that the dated  in question was execute by her clearly understanding the nature of the transaction. In the instant case it is the respondent who seeks to sustain disposition made by Meher Afzan Bibi in favour of her son :Mahtabuddira. The fact that in the meantime Mahtabuddin has transferred the entire property to respondent No, 1 Alijan alias Alijan Bepari does not make any difference in the application of the rule of law as enunciated by the different authorities. The view taken by this Division in the case of Siddique Ahmed Chbwdhury vs. Gani Ahmed, 33 DLR (AD) 1 cannot be said to be a departure from the well-established rule of law as indicated above. However the judgment contains some observations which need clarification to remove the notion that the special rule of protection given to the pardanashin lady is confined to herself only and this benefit is not available to the person upon whom the property might have developed in the absence of the impugned disposition. The relevant portion of the judgment is quoted below; 

 10. Now a question has been raised by the learned Judge that on account of fiduciary relationship the burden of proof rests upon Mahtabuddin who by the impugned deeds acquired 'the entire interest of his mother Meher Afzan Bibi, but the bonafide purchaser from him cannot be burdened with the onus of proof that Mehet Afzan Bibi, the executant of the disputed documents, had independent advice and understood the contents of the said documents. The rule of law as stated above does not make any difference between the person who directly became the beneficiary under the disposition made by a pardanshin lady and the person who subsequent acquired that interest by another transaction, even if it was a bonafide transaction, Respondent No. 2 in his deposition stated as follows:
